exit_trigger: Five-year ROE test fails: ROE falls below 15% in more than 20% of up to ten fiscal years, which signals moat erosion; Negative annual operating cash flow in any of the newest five fiscal years, which signals management or business failure; Price rises above 1.5x the owner-earnings DCF intrinsic value; Evidence that AI or automation is structurally cutting client demand or pricing power for its services; Evidence of dishonest reporting or value-destroying acquisitions
rationale: I own three shares of Accenture, bought four days ago at $251.845, and they are now $226.12, down 10.21%. A price drop of that size, with nothing in the filings telling me the franchise has changed, is not a reason to sell; my own rules say it is the kind of thing to ignore. The snapshot shows a five-year average ROE of 26.9% and debt-to-equity of 0.32, which is the profile of a business earning good returns without leaning on leverage. The model's intrinsic value of $437.57 rests on an 8% growth cap and a 5% discount rate, and I would not lean on a 49% margin of safety built on assumptions that generous. The real question is whether the consulting and outsourcing relationships stay sticky as technology shifts, and I can't prove that from this data, so I keep the position at modest size and keep my eyes open.

exit_trigger: Not applicable; no position is being opened; Would reconsider only if a durable moat is demonstrated with ten-year earnings and ROIC evidence and price offers at least a 15% margin of safety
rationale: I don't own this one, and I'm going to pass. The screen looks nice: a 22.0% five-year average ROE, debt-to-equity of 0.43, and a computed 44% margin of safety. But I can't tell you with confidence where the moat is in a services business whose customers can change vendors and whose work may be reshaped by technology. A business whose moat has to be rebuilt every year is no moat at all. A cheap number built on a 5.94% growth assumption doesn't make up for a franchise I can't see ten years out. We already hold ten names, so the bar for number eleven is high, and this one doesn't clear it. I'll leave it for someone who understands the competitive position better than I do.

exit_trigger: ROE falls below 15% in more than 20% of fiscal years, which would show the franchise test failing; Negative annual operating cash flow reported in any of the newest five fiscal years; Price rises above 1.5x intrinsic value estimate; Evidence of brand pricing power eroding, such as sustained markdowns or loss of market share
rationale: I own ten shares of this company at a cost of $128.38, and they are down about 17% after 105 days. A falling price alone is no reason to sell; the only questions are whether the brand still commands its pricing power and whether management is still allocating capital well. The snapshot shows a 5-year average ROE of about 34.6% and a debt-to-equity of 0.0, which is the kind of economics I like. The DCF puts intrinsic value at $363 per share, but that rests on 8% growth and a 5% discount rate, so I treat it as generous and I'd haircut it heavily. Still, even a big haircut leaves room. I keep the position. I would add only if I became more certain the moat is intact, and the data I have cannot settle that, since it lacks 10-year earnings history, CEO tenure and brand-pricing evidence. Apparel is fashion-driven, which is exactly where moats can slip away.

exit_trigger: Not applicable until a position is opened; if bought later: evidence that ROE falls persistently below 15%; Evidence of customer attrition or loss of pricing power from competing technology; Negative annual operating cash flow or capital allocation that destroys value; Price above 1.5x intrinsic value, with the gap persisting
rationale: I do not own Adobe, and the numbers in front of me are handsome: a 5-year average ROE of 40.0%, debt-to-equity of 0.41, and a price of $228.75 against a computed value of $467.50, which is a 51% margin of safety. But I have spent a lifetime staying away from businesses where I can't say with confidence what the competitive landscape looks like in ten years. Creative software lives in precisely the kind of fast-moving technology I've been wary of, and this snapshot gives me nothing on customer retention, ten years of earnings, or management tenure. A gap that wide between price and my estimate also makes me ask what the market sees that I don't, and my DCF leans on an 8% growth assumption and a 5% discount rate. So I'll sit on my hands, keep this on the list, and wait until I can verify that the moat is not being rebuilt every year.

exit_trigger: Franchise test fails: ROE falls below 15% in more than 20% of the fiscal years measured; Negative annual operating cash flow in any of the newest five fiscal years; Price rises above 1.5x owner-earnings intrinsic value on a persistent basis; Evidence that direct-to-consumer sales or manufacturer policy is structurally eroding dealer economics; Management makes value-destroying acquisitions or buybacks at peak prices, or shows dishonesty
rationale: I own this one, so the question is whether to keep it, and on the evidence I have, I keep it. The snapshot shows a 5-year average ROE of 23.8%, debt-to-equity of 0.40, and a price of $212.82 against an owner-earnings value of $260.01. That is an 18% margin of safety, built on a zero-growth assumption, which is the kind of conservatism I like. My doubt is the moat: a car dealer's edge is largely scale and franchise-law protection, which is thinner than a Coca-Cola brand. The snapshot says nothing about ten years of earnings history, CEO tenure or ROIC, so I can't call this a wonderful business, only a good one at a fair price. I'll hold, I won't add until the moat evidence improves, and I won't sell on a 1.8% paper loss. Price declines are not a sell trigger.

exit_trigger: Moat erosion: 5-year ROE falling below 15% on a lasting basis, i.e. the franchise test no longer passes; Management failure: negative annual operating cash flow, restatements, or evidence of dishonesty; Persistent price above 1.5x intrinsic value; Loss of the sole-source position on a major naval program, or a lasting shift in defense budgets that structurally impairs the franchise; A materially better opportunity at much higher conviction
rationale: I own General Dynamics, and nothing in the snapshot gives me a reason to change that. It builds submarines, combat vehicles, business jets and government IT, and a handful of qualified suppliers serving one sovereign customer is about as regulatory a moat as I can find. The numbers I can check are sound: a 5-year average ROE of 17.2%, debt-to-equity of 0.32, and owner earnings averaging about $3.9 billion against a $94.8 billion market cap. At $350.56 against my $417.18 estimate, the 15.97% margin of safety clears my 15% bar, though only just, so this is no moment to be aggressive. I have owned it for 23 days and am down 0.75%, which tells me nothing. I'll sit and let the business do the work, and I won't add until the discount widens or I can verify the earnings history and management record that this snapshot does not show.

exit_trigger: ROE falls below 15% in a meaningful share of fiscal years, showing the franchise has eroded; Negative annual operating cash flow, a sign management has failed; Price above 1.5x intrinsic value with the gap persisting; Evidence that price-transparent online competitors are structurally compressing gross margins; Evidence of dishonest reporting or value-destroying acquisitions
rationale: I own this one, and I bought it at $120.05 only 25 days ago, so the shares are down 11.7% since. That does not bother me. A falling price is not a sell signal if the business is intact. The snapshot shows a 5-year average ROE of 19.4%, debt-to-equity of 0.33, and a market cap of about $5.9 billion, all of which clear my bar. At $106.01 against an intrinsic value of $129.83 I have an 18.3% margin of safety, wider than when I bought. I will keep the position but not add. The valuation uses a 5% discount rate and 5.1% growth, which is not conservative, and this filing does not give me ten years of earnings or the CEO's tenure. A distributor's moat is scale and service, and it is real but not a Coca-Cola. I want to see more before I press.

exit_trigger: Franchise test fails: ROE falls below 15% in more than 20% of fiscal years, signaling moat erosion; Negative annual operating cash flow reported in any of the newest five fiscal years, a sign of management or business failure; Price rises above 1.5x the owner-earnings DCF intrinsic value and the gap persists; Evidence of pricing power loss from technology or low-cost competition changing how homes are heated; Evidence of dishonest reporting or value-destroying acquisitions by management
rationale: We own this one, and nothing in the snapshot gives me a reason to change that. The business is simple: water heaters and related products, sold through a trade channel that rewards reliability. A five-year average ROE of 23.7% with debt-to-equity of 0.37 is the kind of return on equity I like to see without borrowed money. At $64.90 against an owner-earnings DCF value of $98.59, the margin of safety is about 35%, well above my 15% bar, and the price is nowhere near the 1.5x-intrinsic level that would make me sell. I could not verify ten years of earnings, management tenure or the Treasury-based earnings-yield check from this snapshot, so I am keeping the position at its current size and not adding until I can check those.
